The other day, I found an old shoebox tucked under my bed, its cardboard edges frayed with time. Inside were yellowed ticket stubs from a concert I’d forgotten about, a half-melted chocolate bar from a childhood birthday, and a single, crumpled origami crane my grandmother had folded for me when I was sick. I sat there for a while, turning the crane over in my fingers, wondering how something so small could hold so much weight—memories, love, the quiet ache of growing up.

It made me think about how we carry these little relics of ourselves, even when we don’t realize it. The way a song on the radio can suddenly transport you back to a car ride with your best friend at 16. The scent of rain on pavement reminding you of a city you haven’t visited in years. We’re all just collections of moments, stitched together by things that seem insignificant until they aren’t.

And then there’s the future—a blank page, really. I don’t know what’s waiting for me, but I hope it’s full of the same kind of magic: unexpected connections, laughter that hurts your stomach, and the occasional shoebox of treasures you didn’t know you were saving. Maybe that’s the point—to keep collecting, keep feeling, and trust that the past and future are just two sides of the same coin.

Right now, though, I’m just going to put the crane back in the box and leave it there for a while. Some things don’t need to be rushed.
